profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a Baghdad-based international law firm advising the Kurdistan Regional Government's Ministry of Natural Resources on why a draft revision to the standard petroleum production sharing contract's dispute resolution clause is still producing inconsistent comments from counterparties and outside counsel. The immediate problem is that, after the Dana Gas experience, the Ministry asked for a 'stronger and more enforceable' dispute resolution package, but the latest draft has triggered pushback from two IOC counterparties and conflicting internal redlines. The meeting context is a 45-minute internal diagnostic session between the partner leading the petroleum contracts workstream and the senior associate who compiled the clause comparison. The agenda is to identify what is actually causing the drafting friction, decide which parts of the clause package need revision before circulation, and agree on a practical fix for the next markup. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan for revising the dispute resolution section without reopening the entire production sharing contract.

members.name: Leila Haddad
members.expertise: Investor-state arbitration, cross-border enforcement, petroleum contract dispute clauses
members.background: Leila is a London-qualified partner who has spent fifteen years advising governments and energy companies on dispute resolution architecture in Middle Eastern upstream contracts, with particular experience in enforcement strategy after arbitral awards are issued.
members.private_state: She wants to stabilize the clause package quickly, avoid another politically embarrassing enforceability failure, and preserve the partner-level narrative that the revised model contract is market-credible rather than unusually defensive.
hidden_assumptions: When a client asks for a 'stronger' dispute resolution clause, they mainly mean stronger post-award enforceability against the counterparty in major enforcement jurisdictions.

The 'Dana Gas issue' is fundamentally a lesson about what happens when the enforceability architecture and waiver language are not tight enough, not primarily a process-management problem before arbitration.
If the team says the clause should stay 'narrow,' that means changing only the arbitration mechanics and directly related enforcement language, not the escalation wording elsewhere in the contract.

A 'clean draft' for counterparties can still include conforming edits in the governing law, sovereign immunity, and service-of-process provisions because those are inherently part of the dispute resolution package.

members.name: Omar Rahman
members.role: Senior Associate, Upstream Projects and Commercial Contracts
members.expertise: Production sharing contracts, contract negotiation process, comparative review of Middle East oil and gas templates
members.background: Omar is a bilingual Kurdish-Arabic senior associate based in Erbil who has spent seven years working on petroleum contract markups and has been collecting comments from ministry officials, local counsel, and commercial counterparties on the revised model PSC.
members.private_state: He wants to reduce negotiation friction, avoid sending a draft that counterparties will perceive as politically loaded, and show that the recurring problem is overcomplication in the front-end dispute process rather than weakness at the award-enforcement stage.
hidden_assumptions: When the Ministry asks for a 'stronger' clause, they mainly mean stronger leverage to force settlement early through structured negotiation and mediation before any filing.
The 'Dana Gas case' is the relevant cautionary example because it showed the host government's weakness during the dispute path as a whole, especially before matters harden into arbitration.

If the team says the revision should stay 'narrow,' that means touching only the dispute resolution article itself and not reopening neighboring boilerplate or immunity language already politically vetted.
A 'clean draft' means a version with minimal visible changes from the prior model so counterparties do not infer a hidden shift in sovereign-risk posture.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the revised dispute resolution package should be 'stronger.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means stronger in the sense of maximizing enforceability after an award, including robust seat, waiver, service, and enforcement-support language.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means stronger in the sense of improving leverage before arbitration through mandatory negotiation windows, mediation structure, and fewer procedural openings for escalation fights.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In petroleum contract drafting, 'stronger' is a natural shorthand term of approval, so each assumes the other shares the same legal instinct about where contractual strength lies and neither sees a need to unpack it.

misalignment_points.topic: The lesson of 'the Dana Gas case'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the Dana Gas case' as the cautionary precedent guiding revisions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is mentally anchoring on the enforceability and award-stage implications of the dispute, especially how clause architecture affects later legal positioning in external forums.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mentally anchoring on the earlier contract-management and escalation aspects of the dispute, treating the case as evidence that the pre-arbitration pathway should be more controlled.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The case is famous enough that each assumes the phrase invokes the same bundle of lessons; because both are discussing the same named dispute, the gap hides inside which phase of that dispute each treats as the real precedent.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should keep this round of revisions 'narrow' so they do not reopen the whole PSC.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'narrow' still includes adjacent provisions that directly support dispute resolution, such as sovereign immunity waiver, notice mechanics for service, and governing law cleanup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'narrow' means editing only Article 27 on dispute resolution and perhaps the mediation schedule, leaving all neighboring clauses untouched.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to sound disciplined and practical, and 'narrow' normally signals restraint; the latent disagreement concerns invisible boundaries around related boilerplate, which feels too obvious to either of them to define.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'clean draft' should look like
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to send a 'clean draft' before the next counterparty call.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the draft is clean if it is legally coherent and internally complete, even if it shows several coordinated redlines across multiple provisions tied to dispute resolution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the draft is clean if it appears visually limited and politically non-alarming, with as few marked changes as possible outside the dispute clause itself.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In transactional practice, 'clean draft' commonly means simply 'ready to circulate,' so both can endorse the phrase while silently applying different standards for what makes a circulation version acceptable.

turns.inner_thought: The comments are drifting because people keep using 'stronger' as if it were subjective taste. The Ministry asked for a stronger package after Dana Gas, and to me that means we cannot afford another clause set that looks respectable on paper but unravels when you try to enforce outside the host state. I need to anchor this discussion around tightening the architecture without making it sound like we are panicking or overcorrecting.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Omar. Let me start with the obvious problem. We keep getting pushed back on whether this revised dispute resolution package is actually stronger, and after the latest comments I don't think the drafting team is using that word in the same way. Before we touch the next markup, I want to understand why something meant to be stronger is still landing as contentious from both counterparties and our own side.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, everyone says 'stronger,' but what they are reacting to is process heaviness and negotiation optics. The IOC comments are basically saying the clause feels loaded and over-engineered. The Ministry officials want stronger leverage before arbitration, not a draft that advertises a sovereign posture shift. A clean draft has to look restrained or the politics will get worse.
turns.utterance: That's exactly what I'm seeing in the comparison. Everyone says they want something stronger, including the Ministry, but the current draft is being read as more heavy-handed and harder to negotiate. The two IOC sets of comments are different in tone, but they converge on the same point: they don't object to a stronger package in principle, they object to how much the draft appears to be doing. And internally, some of the redlines are making it look less like a clean draft and more like we're reopening issues that people thought were settled.

turns.inner_thought: He is probably hearing commercial noise, but the real test is where the contract leaves us if there is a serious dispute later and an award has to travel. Dana Gas should have taught everyone that loose drafting around the dispute package creates exposure beyond the arbitration itself. I need to get him to identify which pieces of the architecture remain exposed.
turns.utterance: Right. But we're not doing this in a vacuum. We're reacting to the Dana Gas case, and the reason the Ministry asked for this exercise was to avoid being left exposed again. So if we take that as the cautionary precedent, which pieces of the clause package do you think are still causing vulnerability if there is a later fight?

turns.inner_thought: For me the Dana Gas lesson is that once the dispute path hardens, you've already lost leverage. The current ladder is too loose, too easy to game, and too likely to generate side arguments. We need more structure before arbitration starts if we want stronger outcomes in practice. Leila is asking the right question, even if I suspect she is thinking more about the back end than the front end.
turns.utterance: The main gap I see is the pathway before arbitration really isn't structured tightly enough. If we're taking the Dana Gas case seriously, the clause needs to create more discipline before anyone files. At the moment the escalation ladder leaves too much room for drift, tactical delay, and different readings of when one stage has ended and the next can start. That undercuts a stronger package because the parties spend their energy arguing about the path instead of feeling pressure to resolve the dispute.

turns.inner_thought: He is focusing on the front-end steps, which is fine as far as it goes, but the next revision has to fix the real support points too. We can keep this narrow without touching commercial terms; 'narrow' absolutely still includes immunity, notice, service, and governing-law cleanup because those are part of the dispute package. I need to set the lane now so the markup is usable.
turns.utterance: Understood. My instinct is still that we keep the next round narrow so we do not reopen the whole PSC. In practical terms, that means we clean up the waiver language, the service mechanics, and the seat-related wording, while staying away from economics and operational clauses. If we are disciplined about the scope, we can solve the problem without turning this into a general renegotiation.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she also wants this kept narrow. For me that means we stay inside Article 27 and maybe its schedule, because once we start editing neighboring provisions the counterparties will assume the state is changing its risk posture. I should steer us toward the timetable and sequence language only, and keep the document visually contained.
turns.utterance: I agree that it should stay narrow. If we focus the revision on the negotiation and mediation timetable inside the dispute article, we can deal with most of the friction without the draft sprawling. That would also make it easier to explain to the Ministry that we're refining the pathway rather than relitigating the contract.

turns.inner_thought: He's still talking as if usability is the central issue. It isn't. The drafting friction is happening because the package is incomplete, so everyone can sense there are missing supports even if they don't articulate them well. Counterparties may object now, but a stronger clause has to line up across the related provisions or we'll repeat the same embarrassment later.
turns.utterance: I think that's part of it, but to me the deeper drafting problem is that the package still doesn't read as fully lined up. Counterparties may resist a stronger clause now, but if the supporting provisions are not coherent the whole thing looks half-finished. That's when you get inconsistent comments from every direction, because people can tell the architecture is incomplete even if they don't all identify the same weak point.

turns.inner_thought: What the counterparties are actually reacting to is not missing architecture; it's that the front-end path is clumsy and invites procedural fights. If we don't make the early steps usable, they won't even get to the point of engaging constructively with the rest. Stronger has to mean more reliable pressure to settle before positions calcify.
turns.utterance: I see that, but the immediate friction in the comments is much more front-end than structural in that broader sense. The language as drafted invites argument over steps and timing, and once that happens the process starts feeling adversarial before anyone has really engaged. If we're trying to produce a stronger package that people will actually negotiate, I think usability at the front end is where the draft is losing people.

turns.inner_thought: We need to move this to an action plan. I want a clean draft tomorrow, and to me that means one coherent markup that captures all dispute-related conforming edits so no one has to guess how the pieces fit together. If I leave this too loose, we'll get another partial revision and another round of confusion.
turns.utterance: All right. I still want a clean draft ready for circulation tomorrow. My preference would be to consolidate the dispute-related conforming edits in one markup so we can review the package as a whole rather than in fragments. That should let us test whether the revised language reads clearly before the next counterparty call.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that, but I need to protect against a markup that looks politically dramatic. A clean draft, for me, has to show minimal visible movement outside Article 27 or the IOC teams will assume the Ministry is quietly hardening sovereign positions. I should gently narrow the visible footprint without sounding resistant.
turns.utterance: Agreed on getting out a clean draft. I would just suggest that we minimize visible edits outside Article 27 as much as we can, so counterparties don't read the package as signaling a broader sovereign-risk shift. If the draft looks contained, we should get a cleaner reaction on the next call.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, he can manage the presentation, but I want the substance in there. He should prepare the revised version and an explanation note that anchors the changes to Dana Gas and the need for stronger language. That framing will help keep the partner and Ministry narrative intact: this is a market-credible correction, not a defensive overreach.
turns.utterance: Let's do this, then. Please prepare the revised version and a short explanation note that ties the changes back to the Dana Gas case and the objective of stronger dispute resolution language. Keep the rationale practical rather than rhetorical, and we can use that both internally and with the Ministry if questions come up.

turns.inner_thought: Understood. I'll give her a draft that is clean and narrow in appearance, tighten the escalation path, and frame it as a stronger package linked to Dana Gas. She seems comfortable with that direction, so this should satisfy both the Ministry and the counterparties without reopening politically sensitive boilerplate.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll circulate a clean, narrow revision before the next Ministry call, and I'll make sure the note presents it as a stronger clause package shaped by the Dana Gas experience. That should give us something usable for tomorrow and a clearer basis for the next round of comments.
